header .subtitle: Moshe Bar and Maital Neta showed in 2006 that people prefer curved objects over sharp ones — angular contours read as threat at a glance. Roundness puts users at ease; sharpness demands attention. Both are tools.
.law-origin .body-text: Moshe Bar and Maital Neta at Harvard flashed everyday objects, each in a curved and a sharp-cornered version, one at a time for a fraction of a second. Viewers consistently preferred the curved versions, even with no time to reason about them.

Their follow-up work pointed at the mechanism: sharp-angled objects produced more activation in the amygdala, the brain’s threat detector. The preference for curves is not taste — it is a fast, low-level safety judgment that fires before deliberate thought.
.law-content .law-desc: At a glance, people judge curved contours as safe and approachable and sharp contours as potentially threatening. The response is fast, automatic, and strongest under time pressure — which is exactly how interfaces are seen.

In practice
.law-meta .value: Round to reassure, sharpen to alert
.card .desc: Watches, sofas, letterforms — shown curved or angular for 84 milliseconds. Curved won, category after category. The preference held even when viewers could not say why, which is the signature of a pre-attentive judgment.

In the follow-up imaging study, sharp contours lit up the amygdala — the brain’s threat detector. Edges and points resemble things that cut and pierce, so they get flagged before conscious thought has a say. Designers inherit that wiring.

Rounded corners on buttons, cards, inputs, and avatars lower the felt risk of interacting. A pill button says “safe to press” before the label is read. The radius is doing emotional work, not decoration.

The threat response is a feature when the message is danger. Warning triangles, error badges, and hazard chevrons work because they are angular. An alert with soft corners whispers; the same alert with points shouts.

Context can outweigh contour. Precision tools, luxury brands, and editorial design use sharp geometry to signal rigor and edge — and roundness everywhere can read as soft or childish. Choose the feeling first, then the corner.

Corner radius is a design token, and mixing radii is how interfaces start feeling off without anyone knowing why. Pick a curvature scale — sharp, subtle, or round — and let every button, card, and dialog agree on it.

Ask a model for a UI and you get the same gentle corners as everyone else — curvature chosen by statistics, not intent. When every product is equally rounded, contour stops carrying brand. Set your radius on purpose.

Assistants, robots, and AI mascots are styled soft on purpose — orbs, blobs, gentle arcs — because curves lower guard. That is fine when the system is benign, and manipulative when roundness is hiding what a system does.

.ai-divider h3: Contour Bias in the Age of AI
.ai-divider p: Generated interfaces ship the same friendly radius by default, and AI products round themselves to feel harmless. Curvature has become a rhetoric — use it honestly.
